In this case (resolving massive stellar disks in RF), using instruments across the globe isn't for measuring parallax angles, but to create a radio telescope with an effective aperture the diameter of the Earth. In effect, it creates an interferometer with the resolution of a single instrument with that massive span.

As an aside, there are optical interferometers too (eg Keck on Mauna Kea), but thus far they still have to be in relatively close physical proximity (not yet able to actually record optical waves and combine later as with RF). Fortunately the shorter optical wavelengths provide much finer resolution to offset that.
Do they say what the resolution is, also what is the device they are using to get the image? Film? A CCD?

For RF interferometers, there isn't an imager or film (wavelengths are too long at radio frequencies). The multiple antennae are synchronously swept across an area of sky (sometimes by using the Earth's rotation). The signals are accurately combined (time-wise) and a set of interference patterns results. When combined, the tracks form an image.

Resolution (the finest detail that can be discerned in the pattern) is determined by effective dish diameter, and also by the RF wavelength. There's a rule of thumb to calculate it:

wavelength / effective_diameter = smallest_angle

(smallest_angle is the smallest detectable angular separation in radians)

I don't know what frequencies were used to measure these stars' diameters, so I'll use a known example. ALMA (radio observatory in the Chilean mountains) can operate at 1mm wavelength. Being part of a global interferometer with dishes spaced 7000km apart, the resolution limit is:

10-3 / 7000*103 = 143*10-12 radians

Arc length is equal to distance times angle in radians. So at the star Stephenson 2-18's currently known distance of 20000 light years, that translates to a resolution of:

20000 * 143*10-12 = 2.86*10-6 light years, or around 27 million km.

Assuming I've made no arithmetic errors, that's around one fifty-fifth of the star's diameter - well within the measurement capability of the global interferometer.

As an aside, the Very Large Array (or VLA) in New Mexico is a great example of a radio observatory/interferometer, and a wonderful place to visit.
